title: Liouville's Theorem on Integration: The Gaussian Integral is Not Elementary
description: Formalizes the algebraic core of Liouville's 1835 theorem that ∫e^(-x²)dx cannot be expressed in elementary terms. Proves no polynomial satisfies the Risch ODE p' - 2xp = 1 by a degree-raising argument: the operator L[p] = p' - 2xp raises polynomial degree by 1, so its image avoids all nonzero constants. Introduces differential fields, develops the degree-raising vs degree-preserving operator dichotomy, and axiomatizes the full Risch criterion and Gaussian non-elementarity. The polynomial obstruction (fully proved) is the algebraic core of Liouville's theorem.

meta.author: Liouville (1835), Risch (1969)
meta.assumptions: 5 assumptions: 3 opaque predicates (IsElementaryOver, IsLiouvilleForm, IsElementaryFn — declared opaque since formalizing elementary functions / Liouville logarithmic-sum forms requires differential field theory not yet in Mathlib) + 2 axioms: liouville_integration_theorem (structural form of elementary antiderivatives requires differential Galois/Picard-Vessiot theory not in Mathlib), risch_exp_criterion_gaussian (Risch criterion: ∫e^(-x²)dx elementary iff rational Q with Q'-2xQ=1; requires partial fraction analysis and extension from polynomial to rational case). The Gaussian non-elementarity (gaussian_not_elementary) is now fully proved as a theorem via the iterated Risch operator degree-raising argument.
originalContributions: risch_ode_coeff_top: coefficient identity showing L[p] = p'-C(2)·X·p has coefficient -2·leadingCoeff(p) at degree natDeg(p)+1 — the key lemma driving the degree-raising argument
no_poly_risch_soln: fully machine-checked proof that no polynomial p satisfies p' - 2xp = 1, via the degree-raising operator argument
no_poly_risch_constant: generalization — L[p] avoids all nonzero constants
risch_ode_raises_degree: formal statement that L strictly raises polynomial degree
gaussian_vs_linear_contrast: side-by-side comparison of degree-raising (L₂: Gaussian) vs degree-preserving (L₁: linear exponent) operators, with explicit solutions for the elementary case
DiffField typeclass: basic differential field infrastructure with proved constants_zero/one/add/mul and deriv_neg/sub
risch_linear_surjective_monomial: L₁[Q]=Q'+Q is surjective onto every monomial X^n — proved by induction using recurrence Q_{n+1}=X^{n+1}-C(n+1)·Q_n
risch_linear_surjective_all: L₁ is surjective onto ALL polynomials — proved by linearity (Polynomial.induction_on') using monomial surjectivity

gaussian_not_elementary: fully machine-checked proof that ∫e^(-x²)dx has no elementary antiderivative expressible as a rational function p(x)/q(x). Proof: quotient rule gives f=g·e^(-x²) with f=p'q-pq', g=q²; iterated Risch operator L^n(g)·e^(-x²)=0 (from iterate_derivative_eq_zero); since e^(-x²)>0 and L raises degree (L^n(g)≠0), contradiction. Reduces gaussian_not_elementary from axiom to theorem.

crossReferences.description: Abel-Ruffini for polynomial equations; this is the integration analog — both are Galois-theoretic impossibility results. Algebraic Galois theory (solvable groups) vs differential Galois theory (Picard-Vessiot groups)
Exposes the group-theoretic Abel-Ruffini chain; this entry parallels it for differential algebra — the polynomial degree-raising argument mirrors the A₅ simplicity argument

The OTHER Liouville theorem (approximation/transcendence, 1844). Both are by Liouville but in different mathematical areas: the approximation theorem bounds rational approximation to algebraic numbers; this entry concerns which functions have elementary antiderivatives (1835 result)

Sibling extension of the Abel-Ruffini circle. That entry develops the ALGEBRAIC Galois side (Sₙ solvable iff n ≤ 4, A₅ simple as the obstruction to radical solvability); this entry is the DIFFERENTIAL Galois analog (the degree-raising Risch operator as the obstruction to elementary integration). Both reduce a Galois-theoretic impossibility to a concrete polynomial-algebra fact.

Transcendence of e — the function e^(−x²) whose integral is shown non-elementary here is built from the exponential. Transcendence theory and the theory of elementary functions are the two pillars Liouville founded (he produced the first explicit transcendental numbers in 1844 and the integration theorem in 1835): both ask whether a quantity escapes a prescribed class — algebraic numbers there, elementary antiderivatives here.

Hermite-Lindemann: e^α is transcendental for every nonzero algebraic α. Hermite is a recurring figure in this story — he proved e transcendental (1873) and earlier (1858) solved the general quintic via elliptic modular functions, the canonical example of stepping OUTSIDE radicals/elementary functions to express what Abel-Ruffini and Liouville show is otherwise inexpressible. The Gaussian e^(−x²) is the prototypical analytic function with a transcendental, non-elementary integral (the error function).

overview.historicalContext: Joseph Liouville proved in 1835 (published 1840) that ∫e^(-x²)dx cannot be expressed as an elementary function — a result now understood as the first theorem of differential Galois theory. This predates Galois theory itself becoming widely known, and Liouville's proof was purely algebraic, working in what would later be called differential fields. The Gaussian integral ∫e^(-x²)dx = √π/2 (over all reals) had been known since the 18th century via contour integration and probability, but the impossibility of finding an elementary antiderivative was first rigorously established by Liouville. The modern treatment via the Risch algorithm (1969) transforms Liouville's structural theorem into a decision procedure: given any elementary function, one can decide in finite time whether its antiderivative is elementary. This decision procedure underlies symbolic integration in every major computer algebra system (Mathematica, Maple, Sage). The Risch algorithm's key criterion — that ∫R·e^g is elementary iff a certain ODE Q' + Q·g' = R has a rational solution — reduces the problem of finding an elementary antiderivative to solving a first-order linear ODE over rational functions.
overview.problemStatement: Which functions have antiderivatives expressible in elementary terms? Liouville's theorem (1835/1840) gives a complete structural answer: if f ∈ F has an elementary antiderivative, that antiderivative must have the Liouville form g = v₀ + Σcᵢ·ln(vᵢ) where vᵢ ∈ F and cᵢ are constants. In particular, this theorem implies ∫e^(-x²)dx is not elementary, proved via the Risch criterion: the nonexistence of a rational Q with Q' - 2xQ = 1.
overview.text: Formalizes the polynomial obstruction to the Gaussian integral's elementarity. The core result — that no polynomial p satisfies p' - 2xp = 1 — is fully machine-verified. The proof proceeds by the degree-raising argument: the operator L[p] = p' - 2xp raises polynomial degree by exactly 1 for any nonzero p (proved in risch_ode_coeff_top), so L's image consists entirely of polynomials of degree ≥ 1 and therefore never reaches the constant polynomial 1. The full Risch criterion and Gaussian non-elementarity are axiomatized, with the gap (polynomial → rational case) documented. The differential field infrastructure is developed from scratch since Mathlib has no Picard-Vessiot theory.
overview.proofStrategy: The polynomial obstruction proof is purely algebraic. For any polynomial p, compute the coefficient of X^(natDeg p + 1) in L[p] = derivative p - C(2) * X * p: this coefficient is -2 * leadingCoeff(p) (proved in risch_ode_coeff_top by simp + push_cast + ring). If L[p] = 1, the coefficient of X^(natDeg p + 1) in 1 is 0, forcing -2 * leadingCoeff(p) = 0, hence leadingCoeff(p) = 0 — contradicting p ≠ 0. For p = 0, L[0] = 0 ≠ 1 directly. The Risch criterion axiom then connects polynomial non-solvability to rational non-solvability; full rational analysis requires partial fraction theory not in Mathlib. The elementary contrast (∫e^x dx is elementary) is formalized: for L₁[Q] = Q' + Q, Q = C(c) solves L₁[Q] = C(c) since C(c)' = 0, making L₁ surjective onto constants.
keyInsights: The operator L₂[Q] = Q' - 2xQ raises polynomial degree by 1 (the -2xQ term dominates), so its image avoids all degree-0 polynomials — this is the algebraic core of the Gaussian's non-elementarity
In contrast, L₁[Q] = Q' + Q preserves degree (the Q term dominates Q'), so every constant polynomial is in its image — this is why ∫e^x dx is always elementary for any polynomial integrand
The degree-raising vs degree-preserving dichotomy exactly captures the structural difference between ∫e^(-x²) and ∫e^x as integration problems
The Risch algorithm (1969) reduces the question 'is ∫f·e^g elementary?' to 'does Q' + Q·g' = f have a rational solution?' — an algebraically decidable problem

The polynomial case (proved here) and the rational case (axiomatized) together establish the Gaussian's non-elementarity; the gap from polynomial to rational requires partial fraction analysis showing poles cannot cancel

The Abel-Ruffini analogy is structural: A₅ simplicity (algebraic Galois) corresponds to the degree-raising operator (differential Galois), both witnessing an obstruction to expressibility in a prescribed form

Differential fields — fields with a derivation satisfying the Leibniz rule — are the natural setting, and constants (elements with zero derivative) form a subfield. Mathlib lacks Picard-Vessiot theory for a full machine-verified proof

**Picard-Vessiot theory makes the analogy with Abel-Ruffini exact**: The full Picard-Vessiot framework (Picard 1887, Vessiot 1892, modernized by Kolchin 1973 in *Differential Algebra and Algebraic Groups*) supplies the differential Galois group $G \leq \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ of a linear ODE over a differential field $F$ — an *algebraic group* whose connected component captures the symmetries of the solution space. The Kolchin-Kovacic theorems then sharpen Liouville's structural form: a linear ODE $L(y) = 0$ has all solutions expressible as **Liouvillian functions** (built from $F$ by integrations $\int$, exponentials of integrals $\exp \int$, and algebraic extensions) iff the connected component of its differential Galois group $G^{\circ}$ is *solvable* as an algebraic group. **For the Gaussian**: the ODE $y' - 2xy = 1$ has fundamental solution $y_0(x) = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} \cdot e^{x^2} \cdot \mathrm{erf}(x)$ and homogeneous solution $y_1(x) = e^{x^2}$. The associated differential Galois group over $\mathbb{C}(x)$ is the affine group $\mathrm{Aff}(1) = \mathbb{G}_a \rtimes \mathbb{G}_m$ — solvable! So by Kolchin-Kovacic, $\int e^{-x^2} dx$ *is* Liouvillian (it is built from $e^{-x^2}$ by one integration), it just isn't *elementary*. The exact statement: the Gaussian fails elementarity (Liouville 1835) but succeeds Liouvillianness (because $\mathrm{Aff}(1)$ is solvable). The obstruction proved in this file ($L_2$ raises degree, so 1 is not in its polynomial image) is precisely the algebraic shadow of this distinction: elementary functions over $\mathbb{C}(x)$ correspond to a *strict* subclass of solvable-Galois-group ODEs — namely those with $G^{\circ}$ a torus $\mathbb{G}_m^n$, no $\mathbb{G}_a$ factor. The unipotent additive factor $\mathbb{G}_a$ in $\mathrm{Aff}(1)$ for the Gaussian is what forces the new transcendental $\mathrm{erf}(x)$ — the same group-theoretic structure that, in the algebraic Abel-Ruffini case (this entry's sibling `abel-ruffini-galois-extensions`), forces transcendental modular functions (Hermite 1858) when $S_5$ exceeds solvable.

**The error function erf(x) as the canonical non-elementary special function.** The Gaussian's antiderivative exists as a perfectly well-defined entire function, erf(x) = (2/√π)∫₀ˣ e^{−t²} dt = (2/√π) Σ (−1)ⁿ x^{2n+1}/(n!(2n+1)); it is simply not *elementary*. Liouville's criterion proves erf is genuinely new — not any finite combination of exp, log, sin, cos, radicals and rational operations — in the same precise sense that Hermite–Lindemann (this entry's cross-reference) proves e and π are not algebraic. It is the prototype of a whole family arising the same way: the sine/cosine integrals Si, Ci; the exponential and logarithmic integrals Ei, li (with π(x) ∼ li(x) by the prime number theorem); the Fresnel integrals of optics; and the elliptic integrals K(k) that were Liouville's original 1835 'transcendents'. The Risch algorithm (keyInsight #4) reduces 'is ∫f elementary?' to a decidable algebraic question, and computer-algebra systems return the special-function name (`Erf`, `Si`, `Ei`, `EllipticK`) exactly when the integral is non-elementary.

**The Risch algorithm: from impossibility theorem to decision procedure.** Liouville's 1835 result is structural — it says *when* an antiderivative is elementary (the Liouville form g = v₀ + Σ cᵢ ln vᵢ) but not *how* to find one. Risch (1969) closed the gap with a decision procedure: given an elementary f over ℚ it decides in finite time whether ∫f dx is elementary and, if so, produces it. The method is recursive in transcendence-tower depth — adding one exponential or logarithm at a time and at each level reducing ∫f to a rational-function part (Hermite reduction) plus a Risch ODE R' + R·(θ'/θ) = g. The polynomial obstruction proved in this file (no polynomial p satisfies p' − 2xp = 1) is exactly the base case of the Risch ODE for the Gaussian — the iterated extension of which the entry axiomatizes as `risch_exp_criterion_gaussian`. Risch is implemented in Mathematica, Maple, Sage, SymPy and Maxima; the full Risch differential-equation subproblem is not known to be decidable in every algebraic case (partially resolved by Bronstein 1990), so implementations use a heuristic variant. Formalizing Risch in Lean is the natural extension of this entry: the polynomial obstruction here is the base case, the tower solver the inductive step.

sections.title: Module Header and Background
sections.summary: Module documentation covering Liouville's integration theorem, the Risch algorithm, the core polynomial obstruction, and the elementary contrast. Imports Polynomial.Derivative, Polynomial.Basic, Polynomial.Degree.Definitions, RingTheory.Algebraic.Basic, Analysis.SpecialFunctions.ExpDeriv, and Tactic.
sections.mathContext: The central object: the operator L₂[Q] = Q' - 2xQ (Risch ODE for ∫e^(-x²)dx). Core result: no polynomial lies in L₂⁻¹(1). Contrast: L₁[Q] = Q' + Q (Risch ODE for ∫e^x dx) has 1 in its image.

sections.title: Differential Fields
sections.summary: Introduces the DiffField typeclass (a field with a derivation satisfying Leibniz rule) and proves basic identities: constants_zero (D(0)=0), constants_one (D(1)=0), constants_add/mul (constants closed under +,×), deriv_neg (D(-f)=-D(f)), deriv_sub (D(f-g)=D(f)-D(g)).
sections.mathContext: A **differential field** (F, +, ×, D) satisfies: D(f+g) = D(f)+D(g) and D(fg) = D(f)g + fD(g). Constants are {f : D(f) = 0}. Basic identities proved from these two axioms alone.

sections.title: Liouville Integration Theorem and Risch Criterion (Axioms)
sections.summary: Parts II–III. Declares three opaque predicates (IsElementaryOver, IsLiouvilleForm, IsElementaryFn) since elementary/Liouville-form functions need differential field theory absent from Mathlib, then axiomatizes the structural Liouville theorem (if f has an elementary antiderivative g, then g = v₀ + Σcᵢ·ln(vᵢ) with vᵢ ∈ F and cᵢ constants) and the Risch criterion for ∫e^(-x²) (elementary iff a rational Q satisfies Q' − 2xQ = 1). The Gaussian non-elementarity itself is NOT axiomatized here — it is proved as a theorem in the core-proof section.
sections.mathContext: **Liouville (1835)**: If D(g) = f and g is elementary over F, then g = v₀ + Σcᵢ ln(vᵢ). Requires Picard-Vessiot theory (no Mathlib formalization). **Risch criterion**: ∫e^(-x²) is elementary iff ∃ rational Q/R with (Q/R)' - 2x(Q/R) = 1. **Gaussian non-elementarity**: ∫e^(-x²) is not a rational function.

sections.title: The Core Algebraic Proof — No Polynomial Risch Solution
sections.summary: Part IV, the mathematical heart. risch_ode_coeff_top: coefficient at natDeg+1 of L[p] equals -2·leadingCoeff(p). poly_one_coeff_pos: constant 1 has zero coefficient at position ≥1. no_poly_risch_soln: main polynomial obstruction, by contradiction on leadingCoeff. no_poly_risch_constant: generalization to all nonzero constants. risch_ode_raises_degree: formal degree-raising statement. The section then bootstraps the polynomial obstruction into a full analytic non-elementarity proof: rischOp (the operator L as a polynomial map), rischOp_iter_ne_zero (iterating L keeps polynomials nonzero), hasDerivAt_mul_gauss and risch_iterate_eq (the n-th derivative of h(x)·e^(−x²) equals Lⁿ(h)(x)·e^(−x²)), culminating in gaussian_not_elementary — a fully machine-checked theorem that ∫e^(−x²)dx has no rational-function antiderivative.
sections.mathContext: Key identity: (p' - C(2)·X·p).coeff(natDeg p + 1) = -2·leadingCoeff(p). Proof: coeff(p', natDeg+1) = (natDeg+2)·coeff(p, natDeg+2) = 0 (above degree); coeff(C(2)·X·p, natDeg+1) = 2·coeff(p, natDeg) = 2·leadingCoeff(p). Net: 0 - 2·lc = -2·lc. For gaussian_not_elementary: if d/dx[p/q] = e^(−x²) then p'q − pq' = q²·e^(−x²), i.e. f = g·e^(−x²) with g = q² ≠ 0; differentiating n = deg(f)+1 times gives 0 = Lⁿ(g)·e^(−x²), but e^(−x²) > 0 and L raises degree so Lⁿ(g) ≠ 0 — contradiction.

sections.title: Pointwise Reformulation
sections.summary: risch_pointwise_to_poly: converts pointwise equality (∀x, p'(x) - 2x·p(x) = 1) to polynomial identity using Polynomial.funext (density argument: two polynomials agreeing everywhere on ℝ are equal). no_poly_risch_pointwise: pointwise formulation of the main obstruction.
sections.mathContext: **Polynomial.funext** (Mathlib): If f(x) = g(x) for all x : ℝ, then f = g as polynomials. This uses the fact that ℝ is infinite — a polynomial with infinitely many roots is identically zero.

sections.title: Elementary Contrast: The Linear Exponent Case
sections.summary: Shows that for g = x (linear exponent), the Risch ODE Q' + Q = R IS solvable for every polynomial R: risch_g_linear_const (Q=1 solves for R=1), risch_g_linear_degree1 (Q=X-1 solves for R=X, the ∫xeˣ formula), risch_g_linear_constant_solvable (Q=C(c) solves for R=C(c)). gaussian_vs_linear_contrast packages the dichotomy as a conjunction.
sections.mathContext: For L₁[Q] = Q' + Q: C(c)' + C(c) = 0 + C(c) = C(c) for any constant c. So L₁ maps constants to themselves — the degree-0 case is handled by Q being constant. This contrasts with L₂ where the -2xQ term forces degree to increase.

sections.title: L₁ is Surjective onto All Polynomials
sections.summary: risch_linear_surjective_monomial: for each n, ∃Q with Q' + Q = X^n (induction via recurrence Q_{n+1} = X^{n+1} - C(n+1)·Q_n). risch_linear_surjective_all: L₁ is surjective onto ALL polynomials (by Polynomial.induction_on' linearity). This completes the contrast: L₁ maps onto every polynomial, while L₂ misses all nonzero constants.
sections.mathContext: Recurrence Q_0=1; Q_{n+1}=X^{n+1}-C(n+1)·Q_n satisfies Q_{n+1}'+Q_{n+1}=X^{n+1} by induction. For the full polynomial case, linearity: L₁[C(a)·Q]=C(a)·L₁[Q] and L₁[P+Q]=L₁[P]+L₁[Q] allow reduction to monomials. Together: ∫p(x)eˣdx is elementary for EVERY polynomial p.

sections.title: Abel-Ruffini Analogy and Summary
sections.summary: Documents the structural analogy between Abel-Ruffini (algebraic Galois theory) and Liouville (differential Galois theory). gaussian_risch_polynomial_obstruction_summary: final packaged theorem stating ¬∃p, p' - C(2)·X·p = 1.
sections.mathContext: The pattern: Abel-Ruffini (A₅ simplicity → no radical formula for quintic) mirrors Liouville (degree-raising operator → no elementary integral for Gaussian). Both are Galois-theoretic impossibility results where the obstruction is witnessed by a polynomial algebra fact.

conclusion.summary: Formalization of the obstruction to the Gaussian integral's elementarity. The polynomial obstruction (no_poly_risch_soln) is fully machine-checked: no polynomial p satisfies p' - 2xp = 1, via a clean degree-raising argument. This is bootstrapped into gaussian_not_elementary — a fully proved theorem that ∫e^(−x²)dx has no rational-function antiderivative — by iterating the Risch operator on h(x)·e^(−x²) and using that L raises degree (so Lⁿ(g) ≠ 0 while the n-th derivative vanishes). The linear contrast is also complete: L₁[Q]=Q'+Q is proved surjective onto all polynomials (risch_linear_surjective_monomial + risch_linear_surjective_all), so ∫p(x)eˣdx is elementary for every polynomial p. Two axioms plus three opaque predicates (five assumptions total) cover the parts requiring differential Galois / Picard-Vessiot theory not yet in Mathlib: the structural Liouville form of elementary antiderivatives and the polynomial→rational extension of the Risch criterion. Total: 24 theorems/lemmas, 2 axioms + 3 opaque predicates, 0 sorries, 540 lines.
conclusion.implications: **Theoretical Significance**: Liouville's integration theorem inaugurated differential algebra and the Risch decision procedure (1969), which underlies symbolic integration in all major computer algebra systems. The degree-raising operator argument is a model case of how algebraic structure (polynomial degree) witnesses transcendence. The structural analogy with Abel-Ruffini (both are Galois-theoretic impossibility results proved by polynomial algebra arguments) is formalized explicitly. The formalization also provides a clean pedagogical development of differential field basics and the Risch criterion framework.
openQuestions: Reduce the axiom count: extend the polynomial obstruction to rational functions using partial fraction analysis. Key step: if Q = p/q (in lowest terms) satisfies Q' - 2xQ = 1, then poles of Q' must cancel with poles of 2xQ; analyzing the pole order at each root of q leads to a contradiction. This requires Mathlib's partial fraction decomposition.

Formalize Liouville's structure theorem: prove (not axiomatize) that elementary antiderivatives have the form g = v₀ + Σcᵢln(vᵢ). This requires formalizing Picard-Vessiot theory — a substantial Mathlib project (>1000 lines), but the foundation laid here (DiffField, constants) is the first step.

Generalize to the full Risch algorithm: formalize that ∫R(x)e^(g(x)) is elementary iff Q' + Qg' = R has a rational solution, and prove decidability. This would make the gallery entry a verified decision procedure.

Formalize the explicit integration-by-parts formula: the polynomial Q solving Q'+Q=p is Q=∑ₖ(-1)ᵏ·p^(k) (alternating sum of derivatives of p). This would give an explicit closed-form witness, not just an existence proof. Requires finite sum manipulation in Lean.

Connect to differential Galois groups: formalize the Picard-Vessiot picture for ∫e^(-x²)dx. The differential Galois group of e^(-x²) itself (the rank-1 equation u' = -2xu) is the multiplicative group ℂ* = 𝔾_m, while the inhomogeneous Risch ODE y' - 2xy = 1 has differential Galois group the affine group Aff(1) = 𝔾_a ⋊ 𝔾_m. Both groups are solvable (𝔾_m is abelian; Aff(1) is metabelian), so by the Kolchin-Kovacic theorem the Gaussian integral IS Liouvillian — it is built from e^(-x²) by a single integration — even though it is not elementary. The obstruction to elementarity is therefore NOT non-solvability of the Galois group (the group is solvable, consistent with the Picard-Vessiot keyInsight above); it is the presence of the unipotent additive factor 𝔾_a, since elementary functions over ℂ(x) correspond to the strict subclass of solvable-group ODEs whose connected component is a pure torus 𝔾_m^n with no 𝔾_a summand. Formalizing the 𝔾_a factor as the exact group-theoretic shadow of the degree-raising obstruction proved here would give the full Picard-Vessiot version of the result.

mainTheorems.name: no_poly_risch_soln
mainTheorems.description: No polynomial p satisfies the Risch ODE p' - C(2)·X·p = 1. This is the polynomial obstruction to the Gaussian integral's elementarity.
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ p : Polynomial ℝ, Polynomial.derivative p - Polynomial.C 2 * (Polynomial.X * p) ≠ 1

mainTheorems.name: risch_ode_coeff_top
mainTheorems.description: The coefficient of X^(natDegree p + 1) in (derivative p - C 2 · (X · p)) equals -2 · leadingCoeff(p). This is the algebraic identity driving the degree-raising argument.

mainTheorems.name: risch_ode_raises_degree
mainTheorems.description: The Risch operator L strictly raises polynomial degree: for p ≠ 0, natDegree(L[p]) > natDegree(p).
mainTheorems.leanType: (p : Polynomial ℝ) → (hp : p ≠ 0) → p.natDegree < (Polynomial.derivative p - Polynomial.C 2 * (Polynomial.X * p)).natDegree

mainTheorems.name: gaussian_vs_linear_contrast
mainTheorems.description: Packages the asymmetry: for g=x, L₁[Q] = Q'+Q = C(c) HAS polynomial solutions; for g=-x², L₂[Q] = Q'-2xQ = C(c) has NONE (for c≠0). This is the formalized structural explanation for why ∫e^(-x²) is not elementary while ∫e^x is.
mainTheorems.leanType: (c : ℝ) → (hc : c ≠ 0) → (∃ Q : Polynomial ℝ, Polynomial.derivative Q + Q = Polynomial.C c) ∧ (¬∃ Q : Polynomial ℝ, Polynomial.derivative Q - Polynomial.C 2 * (Polynomial.X * Q) = Polynomial.C c)

mainTheorems.name: gaussian_risch_polynomial_obstruction_summary
mainTheorems.description: Summary theorem: no polynomial p satisfies the Risch ODE for the Gaussian.
mainTheorems.leanType: ¬∃ p : Polynomial ℝ, Polynomial.derivative p - Polynomial.C 2 * (Polynomial.X * p) = 1
